item.message: `[features].memory_tool` is deprecated. Use `[features].memories` instead. (Enable it with `--enable memories` or `[features].memories` in config.toml. See https://developers.openai.com/codex/config-basic#feature-flags for details.)

item.text:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — Undefined measurement methodology.** The bill does not say how computing operations are to be counted, audited, or attributed, including whether failed runs, data preparation, architecture searches, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning count toward the threshold. Companies and enforcers could reach substantially different totals for the same project.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Single training run” invites fragmentation.** A developer could divide training among multiple nominal runs, checkpoints, subsidiaries, or locations, keeping each run below \(10^{26}\) operations while combining the resulting work into one system.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Trained using” is ambiguous for composite systems.** The text does not explain whether the threshold applies to each component model or to the aggregate computation used for an ensemble, mixture-of-experts system, or system assembled from several smaller models.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — Integer operations may sweep too broadly.** Counting all integer operations without defining which operations qualify could include ordinary computing unrelated to model training. Conversely, specialized operations that are not conventionally reported as integer or floating-point operations might escape the threshold.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — Compute alone can miss highly capable systems.** A model trained below the threshold remains outside subparagraph (A), even if algorithmic improvements, synthetic data, tool use, or integration with other models make it exceptionally capable, unless the Secretary separately acts under subparagraph (B).

6. **Section 2(1)(B) — Critical capability terms are undefined.** “Substantially exceeding,” “human performance,” “most,” and “cognitive tasks” supply no benchmarks, comparison population, testing conditions, or required task set. That makes coverage unpredictable and creates a substantial vagueness challenge, especially because criminal penalties attach.

7. **Section 2(1)(B) — No determination process.** The bill gives no procedure, evidentiary standard, notice, hearing, testing authority, or timetable for a Secretary’s capability determination. It also does not say whether a determination covers only the tested version or later copies, derivatives, and updates.

8. **Section 2(1)(B) — “The Secretary” is never identified.** The bill refers to several federal officials and departments but never defines which Secretary makes covered-system determinations. That omission could prevent or invalidate determinations.

9. **Section 2(1) — “Model” and “system” are not defined.** Subparagraph (A) covers a model, while subparagraph (B) and section 3 refer more broadly to a system. The text does not establish when models, software, tools, databases, and hardware collectively become one covered system.

10. **Section 2(2) — The definition of “U.S. person” has major omissions.** It excludes lawful permanent residents, U.S. nationals who are not citizens, partnerships, LLCs that are not treated as corporations, unincorporated associations, trusts, federal corporations, and possibly entities organized in the District of Columbia or territories. Those persons or entities may therefore operate abroad without being reached by section 3.

11. **Section 2(2) — Foreign subsidiaries are not clearly covered.** A separately incorporated foreign subsidiary of a U.S. company is not a corporation organized under state law. A U.S. company could potentially shift prohibited work to such a subsidiary, particularly if the parent’s support does not itself amount to “train, develop, or deploy.”

12. **Section 2 — “Person” is undefined.** Section 3 applies to “any person,” but the bill does not specify whether that term includes governments, partnerships, associations, corporate officers, contractors, or other legal entities. Reliance on background statutory definitions would itself be contestable because the bill does not identify an administering title or agency.

13. **Section 2(3) — “Advanced AI chip” is undefined.** There is no performance, bandwidth, interconnect, age, or export-control standard for deciding which chips count. Facility operators therefore cannot reliably know whether registration is required.

14. **Section 2(3) — The facility threshold is easy to avoid.** A data center with exactly 50,000 chips is excluded because the definition says “more than” 50,000. Operators could also distribute chips among adjacent buildings, campuses, modular units, or legally separate “facilities” because “data center” and facility boundaries are not defined.

15. **Section 2(3) — Chip possession may not reflect usable computing capacity.** The definition apparently counts chips regardless of whether they are installed, operational, networked, or suitable for joint training, while potentially excluding a very powerful facility with fewer than 50,001 newer chips.

16. **Section 3(a) — Core prohibited conduct is undefined.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” could cover everything from preliminary research to offering a finished service, but the bill gives no boundaries. The uncertainty creates both enforcement gaps and fair-notice problems under the civil and criminal provisions.

17. **Section 3(a) — Important forms of assistance are not expressly prohibited.** The bill does not expressly ban financing, selling chips, leasing computing capacity, distributing weights, transferring a system, providing data, publishing instructions, or otherwise aiding another party. General aiding-and-abetting law may cover some criminal conduct, but the text does not clearly create comparable civil liability.

18. **Section 3(a) — Possession and continued operation are unclear.** The provision does not expressly prohibit owning, maintaining, copying, modifying, or providing access to a covered system. Whether continued inference or operation constitutes “deploy[ment]” is left unresolved.

19. **Section 3(a) — Territorial coverage is uncertain for online and distributed work.** The bill does not say where training or deployment occurs when developers, users, chips, and servers are in different countries. A non-U.S. company might serve a covered model to U.S. users from foreign servers while arguing that its deployment occurred abroad.

20. **Section 3(a) — Extraterritorial reach is incomplete and potentially contestable.** It covers U.S. persons “anywhere,” but supplies no rules for foreign subsidiaries, joint ventures, foreign employees, or conflicts with foreign law. Applying severe penalties to conduct with limited U.S. connections could also generate jurisdictional and due-process challenges.

21. **Section 3(b) — The grandfather clause has no completion deadline.** Any covered system whose training “began” before enactment is exempt, apparently forever. A company could commence a token amount of training before enactment and continue the bulk of a years-long run afterward.

22. **Section 3(b) — “Training began” is undefined.** The bill does not identify whether training begins with data collection, a test run, initialization, pretraining, or the first operation in the eventual covered run. Companies could characterize preliminary activity as the beginning of training.

23. **Section 3(b) — The identity of a grandfathered system is unclear.** The text does not say when fine-tuning, retraining, adding tools, changing architecture, or releasing a successor creates a new system rather than continuing the exempt one. This could permit extensive post-enactment development under a grandfathered label.

24. **Section 3(b) — The exemption reaches more than the pre-enactment training.** Because subsection (a) “shall not apply to a covered AI system” whose training began earlier, the exemption can be read to permit not only completion of training but also its later development and deployment.

25. **Section 3(c) — The safety-evaluation exception is unlimited.** It contains no approval requirement, protocol, compute ceiling, time limit, containment rule, reporting duty, or independent oversight. A company could describe otherwise prohibited development or deployment as being conducted for a safety-evaluation purpose.

26. **Section 3(c) — Purpose is an unusually pliable test.** The text does not require safety evaluation to be the sole or primary purpose, so mixed-purpose commercial research may qualify. It also does not assign the burden of proving the exception.

27. **Section 3(c) — Evaluation itself may allow unrestricted deployment.** Because the exception covers “activities,” it could encompass training, development, or real-world deployment claimed to be necessary for testing. There is no restriction on who may access an evaluation system or what happens to the system afterward.

28. **Section 4(a) — “Operator” is undefined.** A facility may have an owner, landlord, cloud provider, hardware operator, and multiple tenants. The bill does not say which party must register or who is responsible when control is divided.

29. **Section 4(a) — Registration has no deadline or required contents.** Operators are told to register, but the bill does not say when, how, or what information they must provide. It also gives Commerce no express authority to prescribe those details.

30. **Section 4(a) — Geographic scope is unclear.** “Each covered facility” could mean facilities worldwide, but the bill does not expressly limit registration to the United States or explain how Commerce can compel foreign facilities with no U.S. operator to register.

31. **Section 4 — Registration is an incomplete enforcement proxy.** Training can be spread among facilities below the chip threshold or conducted at a foreign facility that is difficult to reach. Covered systems can also be created at facilities that do not satisfy the definition, so the registry will not necessarily identify prohibited activity.

32. **Section 4(b) — Reporting content is too vague.** “Describing the computing workloads” supplies no required metrics, level of detail, format, record-retention period, or method for linking workloads across facilities. Operators could comply with descriptions too general to reveal covered training.

33. **Section 4(b) — Certification has no specified standard.** The provision does not say who must certify, what the certification must state, or whether it is based on knowledge, reasonable inquiry, or some other standard.

34. **Sections 4 and 5 — Registry violations carry no stated penalty.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3. Failure to register, report, or truthfully certify under section 4 is not itself assigned a civil or criminal penalty in this bill.

35. **Sections 4 and 5 — No inspection or verification powers.** Commerce receives no express authority to inspect facilities, audit operation counts, demand records, subpoena providers, test systems, or require metering. Self-reported workload descriptions may therefore be difficult to verify.

36. **Section 5(a) — No enforcement mechanism is designated.** The bill does not identify the agency that assesses or sues for civil penalties, authorize administrative proceedings, specify a cause of action, establish venue, or provide injunction and seizure authority.

37. **Section 5(a) — The civil maximum may be inadequate or inconsistently applied.** A penalty of “not more than” $1 million per day allows a nominal penalty and supplies no factors for setting the amount. For a well-capitalized developer, the maximum may be less than the commercial value of continuing.

38. **Section 5(a) — “Each day” does not fit every prohibited act.** Training may be continuous, but development decisions, releases, transfers, or deployments may be instantaneous or intermittent. The bill does not explain when a violation begins or ends, or whether multiple systems and acts produce separate daily penalties.

39. **Section 5(a) and Section 8 — The penalty and effective dates conflict.** Section 5 covers violations occurring on or after enactment, while section 8 says the Act does not take effect until 180 days later. It is unclear whether section 3 is enforceable during that interval, creating both a loophole and a fair-notice problem.

40. **Section 5(b) — “Willfully” is not defined.** Courts use different willfulness standards depending on context, and the bill does not say whether prosecutors must prove knowledge of the system’s capabilities, compute count, legal coverage, or merely intentional conduct.

41. **Section 5(b) — Individual responsibility is unclear.** The bill does not specify when officers, engineers, contractors, or employees are personally liable for a corporation’s conduct. Conversely, a corporation cannot be imprisoned, making part of the stated penalty inapplicable to organizational defendants.

42. **Sections 2, 3, and 5 — Vagueness is magnified by criminal punishment.** The undefined capability standard, undefined conduct verbs, uncertain exceptions, and unclear system boundaries may fail to give regulated parties fair notice or invite inconsistent enforcement. Those concerns are especially serious where violations can result in ten years’ imprisonment.

43. **Section 6 — The international obligation is precatory.** Requiring the Secretary of State to “seek to negotiate” demands an effort, not an agreement, proposal, or result. There is no enforcement mechanism if negotiations never meaningfully occur.

44. **Section 6 — “Equivalent” prohibitions are undefined.** The bill provides no standard for judging equivalence, treatment of exceptions, verification, or penalties. It also says nothing about implementation or Senate approval of any resulting agreement.

45. **Section 7(a) — The termination procedure has no initiating mechanism.** No provision requires the National Academies to prepare a report, supplies funding, sets a deadline, specifies report contents, or identifies who requests it. The statutory condition might therefore never become usable.

46. **Section 7(a) — “Can be developed safely” is undefined.** The bill provides no acceptable-risk standard, evidence threshold, or distinction among types of systems. Congress would have no statutory test for making the finding.

47. **Section 7(a) — “Acting on” a report is ambiguous.** It is unclear whether the joint resolution must adopt the report’s conclusion, merely consider it, or may reach a contrary conclusion. The legal significance of the report is therefore uncertain.

48. **Section 7(a) — The joint-resolution mechanism is underspecified.** The bill provides no expedited procedures or resolution text and does not state expressly that the resolution must be enacted through bicameral passage and presidential presentment. If “finds by joint resolution” were construed as a legislative veto outside that process, it would face a constitutional challenge.

49. **Section 7(a) and (b) — The duration provisions point to different endpoints.** Subsection (a) says section 3 remains effective until Congress makes a safety finding, but subsection (b) ends the entire Act after ten years whether or not that finding occurs. The apparent result is an unconditional ten-year sunset, but the drafting creates avoidable ambiguity.

50. **Section 7(b) — Sunset consequences are not addressed.** The bill does not explain what happens to pending enforcement cases, unpaid civil penalties, registry records, or violations committed shortly before expiration. General savings law may preserve some liabilities, but the bill itself gives no guidance.

51. **Act-wide — No rulemaking authority or administrative framework.** The bill relies on technical thresholds, reports, and agency determinations without authorizing implementing regulations, technical updates, adjudications, or appeals. Agencies may lack clear authority to fill the bill’s central gaps.

52. **Act-wide — No treatment of evasion or aggregation.** There is no anti-circumvention provision requiring aggregation across related entities, coordinated training runs, facilities, or components. Corporate restructuring and technical partitioning could therefore defeat both the compute threshold and facility registry.

53. **Act-wide — No treatment of open-source publication or model transfer.** The bill neither clearly prohibits nor regulates publishing weights, source code, or technical information that lets others deploy a covered system. Attempts to construe “deploy” or “develop” to cover publication could also invite First Amendment challenges.

54. **Act-wide — No allocation of proof for technical thresholds and exceptions.** The text does not say who must prove operation counts, system capability, grandfathered status, or safety-evaluation purpose, or what evidentiary standard applies. Critical facts may be controlled exclusively by the developer, making enforcement difficult.

55. **Act-wide — No protection against obsolete thresholds.** The fixed compute and chip-count thresholds cannot be adjusted for changes in hardware, algorithms, or measurement conventions. Over the ten-year term, they could become either trivially easy to evade or disconnected from the systems Congress intended to regulate.
